issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned judgments convicting the appellant are sustainable in law or not?

facts: The case against the appellant was entirely circumstantial in nature.
The appellant's complicity in the crime was suspected only based on the disclosure statements of a co-accused, who was later acquitted.
No witness placed the appellant at the scene of the crime.
The lower courts had disbelieved the co-accused's disclosure statement in relation to other accused persons.
law: In a case involving circumstantial evidence, the principle for determining guilt is not probability but certainty.
All the evidence presented must conclusively point towards only a singular hypothesis, which is the guilt of the accused.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had applied the wrong legal standard by holding that guilt could be established "in all human probability".

The Court deemed the High Court's reasoning "illogical if not self-contradictory" for convicting the appellant based on the disclosure statement of an acquitted co-accused, especially when that same statement had been disbelieved regarding other accused.
The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had held the prosecution's case to be established in a "perfunctory manner" without properly appreciating the witness testimonies.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction was not sustainable in law because the High Court had applied an incorrect legal standard for a circumstantial evidence case and relied on illogical and contradictory reasoning. Therefore, the Court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court below, while acquitting all the other co-accused in connection with the same crime, erred in not returning a finding qua the instant appellant – a co-accused - in respect of a charged framed under Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860?

facts: The appellant was charged with criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, along with several other co-accused.
The lower appellate court (High Court) acquitted all the other co-accused in the case.
Despite acquitting all others, the High Court upheld the conviction of the appellant without specifically discussing or returning a finding on the conspiracy charge against him.
The evidence on record, at best, only showed that the appellant had concealed incriminating materials, not that he had entered into a prior agreement to commit the crime.
law: The charge of criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code requires an agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act.
To prove conspiracy, it is imperative to establish a "meeting of the minds" between the conspirators for a common object.
A single person cannot hatch a conspiracy; the basic requirement is the involvement of at least two people.
application: The Court applied the legal principle that a conspiracy requires at least two people.
Since all the other co-accused had been acquitted by the lower court, they were deemed innocent of the crime.
This left the appellant as the only person convicted, making it legally impossible for a conspiracy to have existed, as a single person cannot conspire alone.

The Court found no evidence on record to establish a "meeting of the minds" or a prior agreement involving the appellant. The act of concealing evidence, by itself, was not sufficient to prove he was part of a conspiracy.

The Court concluded that the lower court had erred by not properly re-appreciating the evidence and failing to return a specific finding on the conspiracy charge, which was unsustainable once the other accused were acquitted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument, holding that the lower court erred in upholding the conviction for criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B. The conviction was set aside because, with the acquittal of all other co-accused, the fundamental requirement of an agreement between two or more persons was not met, and a single person cannot be held guilty of conspiracy.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the standard for determining guilt is certainty, not probability. The circumstances must be firmly established and, when taken cumulatively, form a complete and unbroken chain that unerringly points only to the guilt of the accused, being incapable of explanation on any hypothesis other than that of guilt and inconsistent with their innocence.
obiter: A finding that 'in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused' is an erroneous application of the standard of proof required in a case involving circumstantial evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's conviction of the appellant is unsustainable because it applied the wrong legal standard to a case based entirely on circumstantial evidence. The High Court erroneously held that the prosecution needed to establish guilt based on 'human probability,' whereas the correct and established legal principle requires certainty, where the circumstances form a complete chain that unerringly points to a singular hypothesis of the accused's guilt and is incapable of any other explanation.
legal_tests_applied: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which an inference of guilt is sought to be drawn must be cogently and firmly established.
These circumstances should be of a definite tendency unerringly pointing towards the guilt of theaccused.

The circumstances taken cumulatively should form a chain so complete that there is no escape from the conclusion that within all human probability the crime was committed by the accused and they should be incapable of explanation of any hypothesis other than that of the guilt of the accused and inconsistent with their innocence.

The principle of determining the guilt of the accused in a case involving circumstantial evidence is not that of probability but certainty and that all the evidence present should conclusively point towards only a singular hypothesis, which is the guilt of the accused.
policy_considerations: An investigating officer is supposed to investigate an offence avoiding any kind of mischief or harassment to either of the party. He has to be fair and conscious so as to rule out any possibility of bias or impartial conduct.
Ethical conduct is absolutely essential for investigative professionalism.
In this case, the Court found that numerous infirmities affected the conduct of the Investigation Officer, calling the credibility of the investigation into question.
